clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of congenital hydronephrosis, producing dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces with a non-dilated ureter below the obstruction
Frequently detected on antenatal ultrasound as unilateral hydronephrosis, though it may present later with loin pain, a palpable mass, infection, or haematuria
Intrinsic causes include an aperistaltic segment or intrinsic stenosis; extrinsic causes include a crossing lower-pole vessel, more relevant in older children and adults

The diuretic renogram (MAG3) is key: an obstructed pattern shows continued tracer accumulation with a rising or non-washout drainage curve after diuretic, whereas a prompt washout suggests no significant obstruction
Differential renal function on renography guides the decision to intervene or observe
Many mild antenatally detected cases stabilise or resolve, so serial imaging and expectant management are often appropriate
Surgical treatment is dismembered pyeloplasty when there is significant or deteriorating obstruction, symptoms, or falling function
reference.pathophysiology: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction is a functional or anatomical impedance to urine flow from the renal pelvis into the proximal ureter. Intrinsic obstruction usually results from a congenitally abnormal, aperistaltic or narrowed segment where disorganised smooth muscle and excess collagen prevent effective peristalsis, so a bolus of urine is not propagated across the junction. Extrinsic obstruction may be caused by an aberrant or accessory lower-pole renal artery crossing and kinking the junction. The resulting rise in intrapelvic pressure and stasis produces progressive pelvicalyceal dilatation and, if severe and prolonged, loss of renal parenchyma and function.
additionalDifferentials: Primary obstructive megaureter (obstruction at the vesicoureteric junction)
Multicystic dysplastic kidney (non-communicating cysts, no function)
Ureteric obstruction from stone or stricture in older patients
additionalInvestigations: Renal ultrasound to grade pelvicalyceal dilatation and assess parenchymal thickness
MAG3 diuretic renogram to assess drainage and differential function
Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to exclude coexisting reflux
CT or MR urography to define anatomy and detect a crossing vessel, especially in adults
Serial ultrasound for surveillance of antenatally detected hydronephrosis
Urinalysis and culture if infection is suspected
redFlags: Declining differential renal function on serial renography
Increasing hydronephrosis or thinning renal parenchyma
Febrile urinary tract infection or pyonephrosis in an obstructed system
Severe or recurrent loin pain, or obstruction in a solitary kidney
reference.prognosis: Many mild antenatally detected cases resolve or remain stable with observation, and pyeloplasty for significant obstruction has a high success rate with preservation or improvement of function; severe long-standing obstruction, however, may leave irreversible parenchymal loss.
pitfalls: Interpreting a diuretic renogram without accounting for a full bladder, dehydration, or an immature neonatal kidney, which can mimic obstruction
Rushing to surgery for mild stable hydronephrosis that would resolve spontaneously
Missing a crossing lower-pole vessel that alters the surgical approach
Overlooking coexisting vesicoureteric reflux before attributing all dilatation to junction obstruction
